title: "Microservices Architecture"

## What you will build and understand

A small shop starts with **Product**, **User**, and **Order** responsibilities. Order needs Product's price and User's identity; the service boundaries become useful only after we understand how to handle remote calls, discovery, failures, security, monitoring, and asynchronous work.

This tutorial develops the *same* shop throughout, rather than switching examples every time a new infrastructure product appears. The lessons explain the concepts in original English prose and use short Node.js or TypeScript snippets where helpful; they do **not** copy the source course's Java implementation.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Run the complete tiny example

A single [shop-lab.mjs](examples/shop-lab.mjs) file starts Product (two instances), User, Order and a simple Gateway. It uses **Node.js 22+ without npm dependencies**:

~~~bash
node system-design/microservices/examples/shop-lab.mjs
curl -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:4100/api/orders?userId=9&productId=7'
~~~

It demonstrates HTTP contracts, simple routing, a timeout, round-robin instance selection, a trace ID and an **in-process** event. It does not pretend to implement real Eureka, RabbitMQ, Zipkin or persistent databases. [Read the lab guide](examples/README.md).
:::

## Study path

1. **[Microservice Foundations](01-foundations/index.qmd)** — Start with a modular shop application. Follow the pressure to split deployments, then confront remote-call failure and learn which components address it.
2. **[Running Case Study: Shop Services](02-shop-case-study/index.qmd)** — Define Product, User and Order boundaries. Keep API contracts small and explicit, then make the first Product HTTP call from Order.
3. **[Service Registry and Discovery](03-service-discovery/index.qmd)** — Replace hard-coded addresses with service identities. Learn the registry lifecycle, why stale entries exist and how Eureka and Consul address the problem.
4. **[Load Balancing](04-load-balancing/index.qmd)** — Give Product two instances and decide where each request should go. Compare client-side versus proxy-side routing, then study the course's Ribbon implementation.
5. **[Declarative Service Clients](05-service-clients/index.qmd)** — Move remote-call mechanics out of Order business logic. Study Feign's declarative contract, then design deadlines, logging, compression and retry policies.
6. **[Resilience and Service Protection](06-resilience/index.qmd)** — Make Product slow and observe the cascading effects. Add deadlines, isolation and circuit-breaker reasoning; compare historical Hystrix with Sentinel and modern alternatives.
7. **[API Gateways and Edge Routing](07-api-gateways/index.qmd)** — Move public URLs behind one entry point. Compare reverse proxies and gateways, then add route matching, filters, authentication and rate limits.
8. **[Distributed Tracing](08-distributed-tracing/index.qmd)** — Trace one browser request through Gateway, Order, Product and User. Learn trace/span context, collection, storage and modern instrumentation.
9. **[Event-Driven Messaging](09-event-driven-messaging/index.qmd)** — Replace a synchronous confirmation side effect with an order.placed event. Learn binders, consumers, groups, partitions, duplicates and delivery guarantees.
10. **[Distributed Configuration](10-configuration/index.qmd)** — Separate operational settings from service binaries. Study Config Server, distributed refresh via Bus, and managed configuration releases with Apollo.
11. **[Performance and Load Testing](11-performance/index.qmd)** — Measure more than successful HTTP responses. Use JMeter concepts, Little's law and an interactive workload experiment to reason about bottlenecks.

## Interactive experiment

Use the [Interactive Queueing Experiment](11-performance/interactive-queue-lab.qmd) to change request arrival rate and service capacity with sliders. It shows why a bounded service needs backpressure.

## How to distinguish architecture from frameworks

| Original course component | Concept it illustrates | Current implementation direction |
|---|---|---|
| Eureka, Consul | Service registration and discovery | Registry or platform-native discovery |
| Ribbon | Client-side instance selection | Spring Cloud LoadBalancer or equivalent |
| Feign | Declarative HTTP client | Current OpenFeign or typed NestJS client |
| Hystrix, Sentinel | Isolation, circuit breaking, traffic rules | Resilience4j/Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker or other suitable tooling |
| Zuul, Spring Cloud Gateway | Edge routing and filters | Supported gateway/ingress implementation |
| Sleuth, Zipkin | Tracing and trace collection | Micrometer Tracing/OpenTelemetry, compatible backend |
| Stream | Broker-neutral message bindings | Functional Stream model or NestJS broker transport |
| Config, Bus, Apollo | Distributed configuration and refresh | Supported central configuration solution |

**Source scope:** The uploaded four-day Spring Cloud course comprises Day 1 (foundations, shop, Eureka, Consul, Ribbon), Day 2 (Feign, high concurrency, Hystrix, Sentinel), Day 3 (gateway, Nginx, Zuul, Spring Cloud Gateway, Sleuth, Zipkin), and Day 4 (Spring Cloud Stream, Spring Cloud Config/Bus, Apollo). Source section mappings appear in each lesson.

::: {.callout-important}
## Technology currency

The PDFs contain historical Spring Cloud component versions and APIs. Those are discussed as **source-era implementations**, not recommended by default for a new service. Links to current official documentation are included in relevant lessons. The independent shop lab is purposefully framework-light and original.
:::

## Mathematical Abstraction

A microservice system can be modelled as a directed dependency graph.

$$
G=(V,E),\qquad E\subseteq V\times V
$$

$V$ consists of Product, User, Order and infrastructure nodes; $(u,v)\in E$ means $u$ depends on $v$ for a specified operation. Edge direction alone does not guarantee synchronous communication.
